title: Deployment & DevOps
summary: Take your code from your laptop to real users: builds, environments, secrets, Docker, CI/CD with GitHub Actions, safe releases, rollbacks, monitoring and Kubernetes.

lessons.title: What deployment means: build vs run
lessons.summary: Learn what it means to deploy software and the difference between building it and running it.

slides.title: From laptop to the world
slides.text:
Your app works on **your** computer. Deployment is the process of putting it on a computer that **other people** can reach.

- Code -> build -> release -> run
- The target is usually a **server** in a data center or cloud
slides.narration: You have written an app and it runs perfectly on your laptop. But nobody else can use it yet. Deployment is everything you do to move that app onto a machine that other people can reach, usually a server on the internet.

slides.title: The build step
slides.text:
**Build** = turn source code into something runnable.

- Install dependencies
- Compile or bundle (TypeScript to JavaScript, C to a binary)
- Minify and optimize assets
- Output: an **artifact** (folder, binary, zip, container image)
slides.narration: The build step takes your source code and turns it into a finished package called an artifact. That can mean compiling, bundling, installing libraries, and shrinking files. The result is something that can run without your editor or your development tools.
slides.code:
npm ci          # install exact dependency versions
npm run build   # create the dist/ folder
ls dist/        # this folder is the artifact

slides.title: The run step
slides.text:
**Run** = start the artifact on a server with real settings.

- Needs configuration (ports, database URL)
- Keeps running, handles traffic
- Can be restarted, scaled, replaced
slides.narration: The run step is when the artifact actually starts on a server and serves users. At this point it needs real configuration, like which port to listen on and which database to talk to. Running is a long-lived job, while building is something you do once per version.

slides.title: Build once, run many
slides.text:
A golden rule from the **Twelve-Factor App**:

- Build **one** artifact per version
- Deploy that same artifact to test, staging and production
- Only the **config** changes between them
slides.narration: A key professional rule is build once, run many. You build a single artifact for each version and promote that exact artifact through every environment. Only the configuration changes. This way, what you tested is exactly what reaches your users.

slides.title: Release = build + config
slides.text:
- **Build**: code -> artifact
- **Release**: artifact + config for one environment, with a version number
- **Run**: start the release

Every release gets an ID so you can roll back to it later.
slides.narration: Many teams think in three stages: build, release, and run. A release is the artifact combined with the configuration for one environment, and it gets a unique version number. Because releases are numbered, you can always go back to an older one if something breaks.

lessons.notes:
## What is deployment?

**Deployment** is the work of taking software from a developer's machine and making it available to its users. For a website, that means putting it on a server connected to the internet. For a mobile app, it means publishing to an app store.

## The three stages

1. **Build** - convert source code into a runnable **artifact**. Examples: a `dist/` folder of HTML/JS/CSS, a compiled binary, a `.jar` file, or a Docker image.
2. **Release** - combine the artifact with the configuration for a specific environment and give it a version (for example `v1.4.2` or a Git commit hash).
3. **Run** - start the release on servers and keep it alive.

```bash
npm ci            # reproducible install from package-lock.json
npm run build     # produce the artifact
node dist/server.js   # run it (in production this is done by a process manager)
```

## Why separate build and run?

- Builds can be slow and need tools (compilers, bundlers). Servers should not need them.
- If you build on every server, two servers might end up with slightly different code.
- A built artifact can be stored, tested, and reused.

## Build once, run many

The **Twelve-Factor App** guidelines recommend a strict separation of build, release and run. Build **one** artifact per version and deploy that same artifact to every environment. Only configuration (environment variables) differs. This guarantees that the code you tested in staging is byte-for-byte the code in production.

## Key words

- **Artifact**: the output of a build.
- **Server**: a computer that runs your app for others.
- **Release**: a versioned artifact plus config.

quiz.q: What does the build step produce?
options: An artifact that can be run
quiz.explain: Building turns source code into a runnable artifact such as a folder, binary or image.

quiz.q: In "build once, run many", what changes between staging and production?
quiz.explain: The same artifact is used everywhere; only the config differs.

quiz.q: Why give every release a version ID?
options: So you can roll back to a known release
Because servers need it to boot
quiz.explain: Numbered releases let you go back to a previous one if something breaks.

lessons.task:
Pick any project you have (or a tiny "Hello" web page). Write down:
1. The exact commands that **build** it and what the artifact is.
2. The command that **runs** it.
3. Which settings would change between your laptop and a real server.

lessons.title: Environments: dev, staging, production
lessons.summary: Understand why apps run in several environments and how code moves between them.

slides.title: One app, many copies
slides.text:
An **environment** is a full running copy of your app with its own settings and data.

- **Development** - your laptop
- **Staging** - a copy of production for final checks
- **Production** - real users, real data
slides.narration: An environment is one complete running copy of your application, with its own settings and its own data. Most teams have at least three: development on their own machine, staging for final testing, and production where real users are.

slides.title: Development
slides.text:
- Runs on your machine
- Fake or sample data
- Debug mode on, detailed errors
- Fast feedback: hot reload
slides.narration: Development is where you write and try code. It uses sample data, shows detailed error messages, and reloads instantly when you save. Breaking things here is totally fine.

slides.title: Staging
slides.text:
- Looks like production: same OS, same versions, similar data size
- Used for final testing and demos
- Catches "works on my machine" problems
slides.narration: Staging should be as close to production as possible: same operating system, same software versions, and realistic data. It is the last safe place to catch problems before real users see them.

slides.title: Production
slides.text:
- Real users and real data
- Debug mode **off**, errors logged not shown
- Changes go in carefully, through a pipeline
- Monitored 24/7
slides.narration: Production is the live system. Debug output is turned off so users never see stack traces, and every change goes through a controlled process. Production is watched all the time with monitoring and alerts.

slides.title: Preview environments
slides.text:
Modern platforms create a **temporary environment for every pull request**.

- Unique URL like `pr-42.myapp.dev`
- Reviewers click and test
- Deleted when the PR is merged
slides.narration: Many modern platforms also create preview environments: a short-lived copy of the app for every pull request, with its own link. Reviewers can click it and test the change before it is merged, and it disappears afterwards.

lessons.notes:
## What is an environment?

An **environment** is one complete, running copy of your system: the app, its configuration, and its data (database, files). Separating environments lets you experiment without hurting real users.

## The usual set

| Environment | Who uses it | Data | Purpose |
|---|---|---|---|
| Development | You | Fake/sample | Write and debug code |
| Test / CI | Automated tests | Throwaway | Run tests on every change |
| Staging | Team, QA | Realistic, anonymized | Final check before release |
| Production | Real users | Real | The live service |

## Parity matters

The closer staging is to production, the fewer surprises. Aim for the **same**:
- operating system and runtime versions (for example Node 24, Python 3.13)
- database engine and version
- configuration shape (same variable names, different values)

Containers (Docker) make parity much easier because the same image runs everywhere.

## Preview environments

Platforms such as Vercel, Netlify, Render and Cloudflare create **preview deployments** automatically for each pull request. Each one has its own URL, so designers and reviewers can test changes before merging.

## Rules of thumb

- Never test with real customer data on your laptop.
- Never debug directly on production; reproduce in staging.
- Production changes go through the same automated path every time.
- Protect production: fewer people can deploy there, and every change is logged.

quiz.q: Which environment serves real users?
quiz.explain: Production is the live environment with real users and data.

quiz.q: What is the main goal of staging?
options: Be as close to production as possible for final testing
quiz.explain: Staging mirrors production so problems are caught before release.

quiz.q: What is a preview environment?
options: A temporary deployment for a pull request
quiz.explain: Preview environments are short-lived deployments created per pull request.

lessons.task:
Draw a simple diagram with three boxes: Development, Staging, Production. For each box write:
- where it runs,
- what data it uses,
- who is allowed to deploy to it.
Then add arrows showing how one code change travels from left to right.

lessons.title: Environment variables and secrets
lessons.summary: Keep configuration out of your code and protect passwords and API keys.

slides.title: Config does not belong in code
slides.text:
Things that change per environment:
- database URL
- API keys
- port number, feature flags

Put them in **environment variables**, not in source files.
slides.narration: Some values change from one environment to another, like the database address or an API key. These should never be written directly into your code. Instead, they live in environment variables that the operating system passes to your program.

slides.title: Reading environment variables
slides.text: Every language can read them:
slides.narration: Every programming language can read environment variables. Here you can see how Node, Python and a shell script each read the same variable called DATABASE URL, with a sensible default for the port.

slides.title: .env files for local work
slides.text:
```
# .env  (NEVER commit this)
DATABASE_URL=postgres://localhost/dev
STRIPE_KEY=sk_test_123
```
- Add `.env` to `.gitignore`
- Commit a `.env.example` with fake values
slides.narration: On your own machine, it is common to keep variables in a dot env file. That file must never be committed to Git, so add it to dot gitignore. Instead, commit a dot env dot example file with fake values so teammates know which variables they need.

slides.title: What is a secret?
slides.text:
A **secret** is config that gives access:
- passwords, API keys, tokens
- private keys, certificates

If it leaks, attackers can act **as you**.
slides.narration: A secret is any configuration value that grants access, like a password, an API key or a private key. If a secret leaks, an attacker can use your accounts, spend your money or read your data. Secrets need extra care.

slides.title: Storing secrets safely
slides.text:
- Hosting dashboards (Vercel, Render, Fly.io) have encrypted env settings
- CI: **GitHub Actions secrets**
- Big teams: a secrets manager (AWS Secrets Manager, HashiCorp Vault, Doppler, 1Password)
- Prefer short-lived tokens (OIDC) over long-lived keys
slides.narration: In production, store secrets in your hosting platform settings or in a dedicated secrets manager, where they are encrypted. In CI pipelines, use the built in secrets feature. Where possible, use short-lived tokens, so that even a leaked token stops working quickly.

slides.title: If a secret leaks
slides.text:
1. **Rotate** it immediately (create a new one, revoke the old)
2. Check logs for misuse
3. Remove it from Git history

Deleting the commit is **not enough**: bots scan GitHub within minutes.
slides.narration: If a secret ever leaks, the first step is to rotate it: create a new one and revoke the old one right away. Simply deleting the commit is not enough, because automated bots scan public repositories within minutes. Then check your logs for any misuse.

lessons.notes:
## Configuration vs code

The **Twelve-Factor App** rule: store config in the **environment**. Config is anything that differs between deploys: database URLs, API keys, ports, feature flags. Code stays identical everywhere.

```js
// Node.js
const port = Number(process.env.PORT ?? 3000);
const dbUrl = process.env.DATABASE_URL;
if (!dbUrl) throw new Error("DATABASE_URL is not set");
```

Failing fast when a required variable is missing is better than a mysterious crash later.

## .env files

For local development, tools like `dotenv` (Node 20.6+ also supports `node --env-file=.env`) load variables from a file:

```
DATABASE_URL=postgres://localhost:5432/myapp_dev
SESSION_SECRET=change-me
```

- Put `.env` in `.gitignore`.
- Commit `.env.example` with placeholder values.

## Secrets

Secrets are config that grants access: passwords, API keys, tokens, private keys.

Good practice:
- Store them in your platform's encrypted settings, CI secrets, or a secrets manager (AWS Secrets Manager, Google Secret Manager, Azure Key Vault, HashiCorp Vault, Doppler, Infisical).
- Give each environment **different** secrets.
- Grant the least privilege needed.
- Prefer **short-lived credentials**. GitHub Actions can log in to AWS, Azure or Google Cloud with **OIDC** instead of storing cloud keys.
- Turn on **secret scanning** and push protection on GitHub.

## When a secret leaks

1. Rotate (revoke and replace) it immediately.
2. Review access logs.
3. Clean history with `git filter-repo` if needed, but assume the old value is compromised forever.

Never log secrets, never put them in URLs, and never send them to the browser: anything in front-end code is public.

quiz.q: Where should a database password live?
options: In an environment variable or secrets manager
quiz.explain: Secrets go in environment variables or a secrets manager, never in code.

quiz.q: What should you commit to Git?
quiz.explain: A .env.example documents required variables without exposing real values.

quiz.q: A key was pushed to a public repo. What is the FIRST thing to do?
quiz.explain: Assume it is compromised: revoke it and issue a new one immediately.

lessons.task:
Take a small project and move every hard-coded setting (port, URL, key) into environment variables.
1. Create `.env` and add it to `.gitignore`.
2. Create `.env.example` with fake values.
3. Make the app stop with a clear error if a required variable is missing.

lessons.title: Static vs dynamic sites
lessons.summary: Know when a site is just files and when it needs a running server, and how that changes deployment.

slides.title: Static sites
slides.text:
A **static site** is just files: HTML, CSS, JS, images.

- Same files for every visitor
- No server code runs per request
- Can be served from a CDN: fast and cheap
slides.narration: A static site is simply a folder of files. Every visitor gets the same HTML, CSS and JavaScript, and no code runs on the server for each request. That makes static sites very fast, very cheap, and easy to put on a global CDN.

slides.title: Dynamic sites
slides.text:
A **dynamic site** runs code on the server for each request.

- Logins, shopping carts, dashboards
- Talks to a database
- Needs a running process (Node, Python, Java, PHP, Go)
slides.narration: A dynamic site runs code on the server every time someone visits. It can check who is logged in, read from a database and build a personal page. That power means you need a server process that keeps running.

slides.title: The middle ground
slides.text:
- **SSG** (static site generation): pages built at build time
- **SSR** (server-side rendering): pages built per request
- **ISR / revalidation**: static pages refreshed every N seconds
- **SPA + API**: static front end calls a separate backend
slides.narration: There is a big middle ground. Static site generation builds pages ahead of time. Server-side rendering builds them for each request. Some frameworks mix both and refresh static pages every few minutes. Another common pattern is a static front end that calls a separate API.

slides.title: How deployment differs
slides.text:
| | Static | Dynamic |
|---|---|---|
| Output | folder | running process |
| Host | CDN / static host | server, container, functions |
| Cost | often free | pay for compute |
| Scaling | automatic | must plan it |
slides.narration: For deployment the difference is big. A static site is a folder you upload, often for free. A dynamic site needs compute that runs your code, so you pay for servers or functions and need to think about scaling and monitoring.

slides.title: Pick the simplest thing
slides.text:
Blog, docs, portfolio, landing page -> **static**

User accounts, payments, real-time data -> **dynamic** (or static front end + API)
slides.narration: The professional habit is to choose the simplest option that works. Blogs, documentation and portfolios are perfect as static sites. Once you need accounts, payments or live data, add a backend, often as a separate API.

lessons.notes:
## Static sites

A static site is a set of pre-made files. The server only reads them from disk (or a CDN cache) and sends them. Tools that generate static sites include **Astro**, **Hugo**, **Eleventy**, **Jekyll**, and static exports of **Next.js** or **Vite** apps.

Pros: very fast, nearly free, highly secure (no server code to hack), scales automatically.
Cons: no per-user logic on the server.

## Dynamic sites

A dynamic site runs server code for each request: Express or Fastify (Node), Django or FastAPI (Python), Spring Boot (Java), Laravel (PHP), Rails (Ruby), and so on. It can read databases, check sessions, and personalize pages.

Pros: full flexibility. Cons: you must run, secure, scale and pay for compute.

## Rendering strategies

- **SSG** - render pages at build time.
- **SSR** - render pages on each request.
- **ISR / revalidate** - static pages rebuilt in the background after a time limit.
- **CSR / SPA** - browser renders everything using JavaScript, data from an API.
- **Edge rendering** - SSR run in data centers close to the user (Cloudflare Workers, Vercel/Netlify edge functions).

## Deployment impact

```bash
# Static: build, then upload a folder
npm run build          # -> dist/
# upload dist/ to GitHub Pages, Netlify, Cloudflare Pages...

# Dynamic: build, then start a long-running process
npm run build
node dist/server.js    # listens on $PORT
```

A dynamic app needs: a process manager or container, environment variables, logs, health checks, and a database. A static app needs a host and a domain.

Rule: start static whenever you can; add server parts only where you need them.

quiz.q: Which is a typical static site?
quiz.explain: A portfolio shows the same content to everyone and suits static hosting.

quiz.q: What does SSR mean?
quiz.explain: Server-side rendering builds the HTML on the server for each request.

quiz.q: Why are static sites cheap to host?
options: No server code runs per request; files can be cached on a CDN
quiz.explain: Serving cached files needs very little compute.

lessons.task: List five websites you use. For each, decide if it is static, dynamic, or a static front end plus API, and explain why in one sentence.

lessons.title: Git-based deploys
lessons.summary: Deploy automatically every time you push to a branch.

slides.title: Push to deploy
slides.text:
Connect your Git repository to a host. Then:

`git push` -> host builds -> new version is live

No manual uploading, no FTP.
slides.narration: Git based deployment means your hosting platform watches your repository. When you push new commits, it automatically builds and deploys them. No more dragging files onto a server by hand.

slides.title: Branches map to environments
slides.text:
- `main` -> production
- `develop` or `staging` -> staging
- any pull request -> preview URL
slides.narration: A common setup is to map branches to environments. The main branch goes to production, a staging branch goes to staging, and every pull request gets its own preview link.

slides.title: A typical flow
slides.text: The everyday commands:
slides.narration: Here is the everyday flow. You create a branch, commit your work, push it and open a pull request. The platform deploys a preview. When the pull request is reviewed and merged into main, production updates automatically.
slides.code:
git switch -c feature/contact-form
# ...edit files...
git add .
git commit -m "Add contact form"
git push -u origin feature/contact-form
# open a pull request -> preview deploy
# merge into main     -> production deploy

slides.title: Build settings
slides.text:
The host needs to know:
- **Build command**: `npm run build`
- **Output folder**: `dist`
- **Runtime version**: Node 24, Python 3.13...
- **Environment variables**
slides.narration: When you connect a repository, you tell the host a few things: the build command, the output folder, the runtime version and the environment variables. Most platforms detect popular frameworks and fill these in for you.

slides.title: Git is your history
slides.text:
- Every deploy maps to a **commit**
- Want the old version? Redeploy an older commit
- Protect `main`: require reviews and passing checks
slides.narration: Because every deploy is tied to a commit, Git becomes your deployment history. Rolling back can be as simple as redeploying an older commit. Protect your main branch so that only reviewed and tested code can reach production.

lessons.notes:
## The idea

With **Git-based deployment** (sometimes called *push-to-deploy* or *GitOps* when it drives infrastructure), the Git repository is the single source of truth. Hosting platforms such as **Vercel, Netlify, Cloudflare Pages, Render, Railway, Fly.io** and **GitHub Pages** can watch a repository and deploy on every push.

## Typical branch strategy

| Branch | Deploys to |
|---|---|
| `main` | production |
| `staging` | staging (optional) |
| pull requests | preview URLs |

## The flow

```bash
git switch -c fix/typo
git commit -am "Fix typo on pricing page"
git push -u origin fix/typo
# Open a pull request -> preview deployment with its own URL
# Review, checks pass, merge -> production deployment
```

## What the platform needs

- **Build command**, for example `npm run build`
- **Output directory**, for example `dist` or `build`
- **Install command** (usually auto-detected from the lock file)
- **Runtime version** (pin it: `.nvmrc`, `engines` in package.json, `.python-version`)
- **Environment variables** per environment

## Protect production

On GitHub, use **branch protection rules** or **rulesets** on `main`:
- require a pull request and at least one review,
- require status checks (tests, lint) to pass,
- block force-pushes.

## GitOps

At larger scale, **GitOps** tools (Argo CD, Flux) apply the same idea to infrastructure: the desired state of the servers is stored in Git, and a controller makes the real system match it. Changing production means merging a pull request.

quiz.q: In a Git-based deploy, what usually triggers a production deploy?
options: Merging or pushing to the main branch
quiz.explain: The platform watches main and deploys when it changes.

quiz.q: What does a pull request often get on modern hosts?
quiz.explain: Preview deployments let reviewers test the change.

quiz.q: How can you roll back with Git-based deploys?
quiz.explain: Every deploy maps to a commit, so redeploying an older one restores it.

lessons.task: Create a tiny static site (one `index.html`) in a GitHub repository and connect it to a free static host (GitHub Pages, Netlify, Vercel or Cloudflare Pages). Change the page, push, and watch it update automatically. Then open a pull request and find the preview URL.

lessons.title: Docker basics
lessons.summary: Package an app and everything it needs into a container image that runs the same everywhere.

slides.title: "Works on my machine"
slides.text:
Apps break on servers because of different:
- OS and library versions
- runtime versions
- missing system packages

**Containers** package the app **with** its environment.
slides.narration: The classic deployment problem is: it works on my machine. The server has a different operating system, a different runtime version, or a missing library. Containers solve this by packaging your app together with everything it needs.

slides.title: Image vs container
slides.text:
- **Image**: a read-only template (app + runtime + libraries)
- **Container**: a running instance of an image
- **Registry**: where images are stored (Docker Hub, GitHub Container Registry, ECR)
slides.narration: Two words to learn. An image is a frozen template that holds your app, its runtime and its libraries. A container is a running copy of that image. Images are stored and shared through registries such as Docker Hub or the GitHub Container Registry.

slides.title: A Dockerfile
slides.text: Instructions to build an image:
slides.narration: A Dockerfile is a recipe for building an image. This one starts from an official Node image, copies the dependency list, installs packages, copies the code, builds it, and says which command starts the app. Notice that dependencies are copied first so Docker can cache that slow step.
slides.code:
FROM node:24-slim
WORKDIR /app
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci
COPY . .
RUN npm run build
ENV NODE_ENV=production
EXPOSE 3000
USER node
CMD ["node", "dist/server.js"]

slides.title: Build and run
slides.text: Core commands:
slides.narration: You build an image with docker build and give it a name and tag. Then docker run starts a container. The dash p flag connects port 3000 on your machine to port 3000 in the container, and dash e passes an environment variable.
slides.code:
docker build -t myapp:1.0 .
docker run -p 3000:3000 -e DATABASE_URL=... myapp:1.0
docker ps            # list running containers
docker logs <id>     # see output
docker stop <id>

slides.title: Containers vs virtual machines
slides.text:
- **VM**: full guest OS, heavier, boots in a minute
- **Container**: shares the host kernel, light, starts in seconds
- Both isolate apps; containers are the standard unit of deployment today
slides.narration: Containers are often compared to virtual machines. A virtual machine includes a whole operating system, while a container shares the host kernel, so it is much lighter and starts in seconds. That is why containers became the standard way to ship server apps.

slides.title: Docker Compose for local stacks
slides.text:
`compose.yaml` runs several containers together:

```yaml
services:
  web:
    build: .
    ports: ["3000:3000"]
  db:
    image: postgres:17
```
`docker compose up`
slides.narration: Real apps often need a database and other services. Docker Compose lets you describe them all in one file and start them with a single command, docker compose up. It is perfect for local development and small servers.

lessons.notes:
## Why containers?

A **container** bundles an application with its runtime, libraries and settings, isolated from other processes. The same image runs identically on a laptop, a CI runner, or a cloud server. Docker made containers popular; today images follow the open **OCI** standard and also run on Podman, containerd and Kubernetes.

## Key terms

- **Image** - read-only template built from a `Dockerfile`, made of cached layers.
- **Container** - a running instance of an image.
- **Registry** - stores images: Docker Hub, GitHub Container Registry (`ghcr.io`), Amazon ECR, Google Artifact Registry.
- **Tag** - a version label like `myapp:1.4.2`. Avoid relying on `latest` in production.

## A good Dockerfile

```dockerfile
FROM node:24-slim
WORKDIR /app
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci --omit=dev
COPY . .
ENV NODE_ENV=production
EXPOSE 3000
USER node
CMD ["node", "server.js"]
```

Tips:
- Use small official base images (`-slim`, `alpine`, or distroless).
- Copy dependency files first so the install layer is cached.
- Add a `.dockerignore` (`node_modules`, `.git`, `.env`).
- Run as a non-root user.
- Use **multi-stage builds** to keep build tools out of the final image.
- Never bake secrets into images; pass them at run time.

## Everyday commands

```bash
docker build -t myapp:1.0 .
docker run -d -p 8080:3000 --name web myapp:1.0
docker logs -f web
docker exec -it web sh
docker push ghcr.io/me/myapp:1.0
```

## Compose

`docker compose up -d` starts every service in `compose.yaml` (web app, database, cache) on a shared network, so `web` can reach the database at host name `db`.

quiz.q: What is the difference between an image and a container?
options: An image is a template; a container is a running instance of it
A container is stored in a registry; an image runs
An image is a virtual machine
quiz.explain: Images are templates; containers are running instances.

quiz.q: Why copy package*.json before the rest of the code in a Dockerfile?
options: So the dependency install layer is cached when only code changes
quiz.explain: Layer caching skips reinstalling dependencies if they did not change.

quiz.q: What does `-p 8080:3000` do?
options: Maps host port 8080 to container port 3000
quiz.explain: The format is host:container.

lessons.task: If Docker Desktop (or Podman) is installed: write a Dockerfile for a tiny web app, build it with `docker build -t hello:1 .`, run it with `docker run -p 8080:3000 hello:1`, and open http://localhost:8080. If not, write the Dockerfile on paper and explain what each line does.

lessons.title: Kubernetes overview
lessons.summary: See how Kubernetes runs many containers across many servers, and when you actually need it.

slides.title: Too many containers
slides.text:
One server, one container: easy.

50 services x 3 copies x many servers?
- Which server runs what?
- What if a server dies?
- How do containers find each other?
slides.narration: Running one container on one server is easy. But a large system might run fifty services, each with several copies, across many servers. Someone has to decide where each container runs, restart them when they crash, and connect them together. That job is called orchestration.

slides.title: What Kubernetes does
slides.text:
**Kubernetes (K8s)** is a container orchestrator:
- schedules containers onto machines (nodes)
- restarts failed ones (self-healing)
- scales up and down
- rolling updates and rollbacks
- service discovery and load balancing
slides.narration: Kubernetes, often written K eight S, is the most popular container orchestrator. You tell it what you want running, and it places containers on machines, restarts them if they fail, scales them, and rolls out new versions gradually.

slides.title: Core objects
slides.text:
- **Pod**: one or more containers together
- **Deployment**: keeps N pod replicas running
- **Service**: stable address in front of pods
- **Ingress / Gateway**: routes outside HTTP traffic in
- **ConfigMap / Secret**: configuration
slides.narration: A few objects cover most of Kubernetes. A pod wraps one or more containers. A deployment keeps a chosen number of pods running. A service gives those pods one stable address. An ingress or gateway lets web traffic in from outside, and config maps and secrets hold configuration.

slides.title: Declarative YAML
slides.text: You declare the **desired state**:
slides.narration: Kubernetes is declarative. Instead of giving step by step commands, you write the state you want, here three replicas of version one point four, and Kubernetes continuously works to make reality match it.
slides.code:
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: web
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels: {app: web}
  template:
    metadata:
      labels: {app: web}
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: web
        image: ghcr.io/me/web:1.4.0
        ports: [{containerPort: 3000}]

slides.title: Do you need it?
slides.text:
- Small app, small team -> **no**. Use a PaaS, a VPS, or serverless.
- Many services, big scale, platform team -> **maybe**
- Use managed K8s: **EKS, GKE, AKS**, DigitalOcean, Linode
slides.narration: Kubernetes is powerful but complex. For a small app or a small team, a platform as a service, a single server, or serverless is usually a better choice. If you do need Kubernetes, use a managed service from a cloud provider so you do not have to run the control plane yourself.

lessons.notes:
## Orchestration

When you run many containers on many machines you need something to **schedule** them, **heal** failures, **scale**, **update** them safely and **connect** them. That is a container **orchestrator**. **Kubernetes** (originally from Google, now run by the CNCF) is the industry standard.

## Architecture in one minute

- **Cluster** = a **control plane** (API server, scheduler, etcd database, controllers) + **worker nodes**.
- Each node runs a **kubelet** agent and a container runtime (containerd or CRI-O).
- You talk to the API server with `kubectl` or with YAML files applied by a CI/CD or GitOps tool.

## Core objects

| Object | Purpose |
|---|---|
| Pod | smallest unit; one or more containers sharing network |
| Deployment | keeps N identical pods, does rolling updates |
| Service | stable virtual IP / DNS name for a set of pods |
| Ingress / Gateway API | HTTP routing from outside into Services |
| ConfigMap, Secret | configuration and sensitive values |
| HorizontalPodAutoscaler | scales replicas based on load |

```bash
kubectl apply -f deployment.yaml
kubectl get pods
kubectl rollout status deployment/web
kubectl rollout undo deployment/web     # roll back
```

## Desired state

Kubernetes is **declarative**: you describe *what* should exist, and controllers loop forever to make reality match. Delete a pod and the Deployment creates a new one.

## When to use it

Kubernetes shines for organizations with many services and a team to run the platform. For a single app it is usually overkill. Simpler options: a PaaS (Render, Railway, Fly.io, Heroku), container services (Google Cloud Run, AWS App Runner/ECS, Azure Container Apps), or a VPS with Docker Compose. If you use Kubernetes, prefer a managed offering (EKS, GKE, AKS). For local learning, try **kind**, **minikube** or **k3d**.

quiz.q: What is a Pod?
options: The smallest deployable unit, wrapping one or more containers
quiz.explain: A pod groups one or more containers that share networking.

quiz.q: What does a Deployment object do?
options: Keeps a desired number of identical pods running and updates them
quiz.explain: Deployments manage replicas and rolling updates.

quiz.q: For a single small web app with one developer, what is usually the best choice?
options: A PaaS, VPS or serverless platform
quiz.explain: Kubernetes adds complexity that a small app rarely needs.

lessons.task: Read the Deployment YAML from this lesson and answer: how many copies will run, which image is used, and which port the container listens on. Bonus: install `kind` or `minikube`, apply the file, and run `kubectl get pods`.

lessons.title: CI/CD pipelines explained
lessons.summary: Understand continuous integration, continuous delivery and continuous deployment.

slides.title: The problem
slides.text:
Manual releases are:
- slow
- error-prone (forgot a step?)
- scary, so done rarely
- big, so they break more

**Automate** the path from commit to production.
slides.narration: When releases are manual, people forget steps, they take a long time, and they feel scary, so teams do them rarely. Rare releases are big, and big releases break more. The fix is to automate the path from a commit to production.

slides.title: Continuous Integration (CI)
slides.text:
Every push or pull request automatically:
- installs dependencies
- runs linters and type checks
- runs tests
- builds the artifact

Red build = do not merge.
slides.narration: Continuous integration means every push or pull request is automatically checked. A server installs dependencies, runs linters and tests, and builds the app. If anything fails, the build turns red and the change should not be merged.

slides.title: Continuous Delivery vs Deployment
slides.text:
- **Continuous Delivery**: every green build is *ready* to release; a human clicks **deploy**
- **Continuous Deployment**: every green build on `main` goes to production **automatically**
slides.narration: CD has two meanings. Continuous delivery means every passing build is ready to release, but a person presses the button. Continuous deployment goes one step further: every passing change on main is released automatically, with no human step.

slides.title: A pipeline
slides.text:
```
push -> lint -> test -> build -> deploy staging
     -> smoke tests -> (approval) -> deploy production
```
Each stage is a **job**; a failure stops the line.
slides.narration: A pipeline is a chain of stages. A typical one lints, tests and builds, deploys to staging, runs quick smoke tests, maybe waits for approval, and then deploys to production. If any stage fails, everything after it stops.

slides.title: Popular tools
slides.text:
- **GitHub Actions** (built into GitHub)
- GitLab CI/CD
- Jenkins (self-hosted veteran)
- CircleCI, Buildkite, Azure Pipelines
- Argo CD / Flux for GitOps delivery to Kubernetes
slides.narration: There are many CI CD tools. GitHub Actions is built into GitHub and very popular. GitLab has its own built in CI, Jenkins is a long running self-hosted option, and Argo CD and Flux handle GitOps delivery to Kubernetes.

lessons.notes:
## CI: Continuous Integration

Developers merge small changes often into a shared branch. Each change is **verified automatically**: install, lint, type-check, unit tests, build. Benefits: bugs found within minutes, the main branch always works, and nobody is afraid to merge.

## CD: two meanings

- **Continuous Delivery** - every change that passes CI produces a release candidate that *can* be deployed with one click (often with a manual approval for production).
- **Continuous Deployment** - every change that passes CI on `main` is deployed to production automatically.

## Anatomy of a pipeline

| Stage | Examples |
|---|---|
| Checkout | get the commit |
| Install | `npm ci`, `pip install -r requirements.txt` |
| Quality | lint, format check, type check, security scan |
| Test | unit, integration tests |
| Build | bundle, compile, `docker build` |
| Publish | push image to a registry, upload artifact |
| Deploy | staging, then production |
| Verify | smoke tests, health checks |

## Principles

- **Fast feedback**: keep CI under ~10 minutes; run slow tests in parallel.
- **Same artifact** is promoted from staging to production.
- **Fail early**: cheap checks first.
- **Reproducible**: pinned versions, lock files, clean runners.
- **Secure**: secrets in the CI secret store, least-privilege tokens, pin third-party actions.

## DORA metrics

Teams measure delivery with four classic **DORA metrics**: deployment frequency, lead time for changes, change failure rate, and time to restore service. Good CI/CD improves all four: deploy more often, with fewer failures, and recover faster.

quiz.q: What does Continuous Integration do on every push?
options: Automatically lints, tests and builds the code
quiz.explain: CI verifies every change automatically.

quiz.q: Continuous Deployment means...
options: A human must approve every release
Every passing change on main goes to production automatically
quiz.explain: No manual step: green changes ship automatically.

quiz.q: Which stage should run first in a pipeline?
options: Cheap checks like lint and unit tests
quiz.explain: Fail early with fast, cheap checks.

lessons.task: Design a pipeline for a small web app on paper. List each stage in order, what command it runs, and what happens if it fails. Mark which stages need secrets.

lessons.title: GitHub Actions in practice
lessons.summary: Write a real CI/CD workflow in YAML that tests, builds and deploys your app.

slides.title: Workflows live in your repo
slides.text:
`.github/workflows/ci.yml`

- **Workflow**: the whole automation
- **Trigger** (`on`): push, pull_request, schedule, manual
- **Job**: runs on a fresh virtual machine (runner)
- **Step**: one command or reusable **action**
slides.narration: GitHub Actions workflows are YAML files stored in the dot github slash workflows folder. A workflow has triggers, which say when it runs. It contains jobs, each running on a fresh virtual machine called a runner, and each job is a list of steps.

slides.title: A CI workflow
slides.text: Test on every push and pull request:
slides.narration: Here is a complete CI workflow. It runs on pushes to main and on pull requests. It checks out the code, installs Node twenty four with caching, installs dependencies, and runs the linter, the tests and the build.
slides.code:
name: CI
on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
  pull_request:
jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v5
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v5
        with:
          node-version: 24
          cache: npm
      - run: npm ci
      - run: npm run lint
      - run: npm test
      - run: npm run build

slides.title: Adding a deploy job
slides.text: Deploy only after tests pass, only on `main`:
slides.narration: To deploy, add a second job. Needs test means it only starts after the test job succeeds. The if line limits it to the main branch, and the environment called production can require approval. The secret is read from GitHub secrets, never written in the file.
slides.code:
deploy:
    needs: test
    if: github.ref == 'refs/heads/main'
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    environment: production
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v5
      - run: ./scripts/deploy.sh
        env:
          DEPLOY_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.DEPLOY_TOKEN }}

slides.title: Secrets and environments
slides.text:
- Settings -> Secrets and variables -> Actions
- Use with `${{ secrets.NAME }}`; values are masked in logs
- **Environments** add protection: required reviewers, wait timers, branch limits
- Cloud login without keys: **OIDC** (`permissions: id-token: write`)
slides.narration: Secrets are added in the repository settings and used with the secrets expression. GitHub hides their values in logs. Environments add protection, such as requiring a reviewer before production. For cloud providers, OIDC lets the workflow log in without storing any long lived keys at all.

slides.title: Good habits
slides.text:
- Set minimal `permissions:` (e.g. `contents: read`)
- Pin third-party actions to a full commit SHA
- Use a **matrix** to test several versions
- Cache dependencies
- Use `concurrency:` to cancel outdated runs
slides.narration: A few good habits keep workflows fast and safe. Give the workflow only the permissions it needs. Pin third party actions to an exact commit, because tags can be moved. Use a matrix to test several versions, caching to save time, and concurrency to cancel old runs when you push again.

lessons.notes:
## Structure

```yaml
name: CI/CD
on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
  pull_request:
permissions:
  contents: read
concurrency:
  group: ${{ github.workflow }}-${{ github.ref }}
  cancel-in-progress: true
jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    strategy:
      matrix:
        node: [22, 24]
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v5
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v5
        with:
          node-version: ${{ matrix.node }}
          cache: npm
      - run: npm ci
      - run: npm test
  deploy:
    needs: test
    if: github.ref == 'refs/heads/main'
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    environment: production
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v5
      - run: ./scripts/deploy.sh
        env:
          DEPLOY_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.DEPLOY_TOKEN }}
```

## Key ideas

- **Triggers** (`on`): `push`, `pull_request`, `schedule` (cron), `workflow_dispatch` (manual button), `release`.
- **Jobs** run in parallel by default; `needs:` makes them sequential.
- **Runners**: GitHub-hosted (`ubuntu-latest`, `windows-latest`, `macos-latest`) or self-hosted.
- **Actions**: reusable steps from the Marketplace, e.g. `actions/checkout`, `docker/build-push-action`.
- **Artifacts**: `actions/upload-artifact` passes build output between jobs.

## Security checklist

- Least-privilege `permissions:` at the top.
- Secrets only via `${{ secrets.X }}`; never `echo` them.
- Pin third-party actions to a commit SHA (`uses: owner/action@<sha>`); tags can be moved.
- Be careful with `pull_request_target`: it runs with secrets on code from forks.
- Use **OIDC** to authenticate to AWS, Azure or Google Cloud instead of storing cloud keys.

Public repositories get free minutes on standard GitHub-hosted runners; private repositories get a monthly free quota depending on plan.

quiz.q: Where do GitHub Actions workflow files live?
quiz.explain: Workflows must be in .github/workflows/.

quiz.q: What does `needs: test` do on a job?
options: Makes the job wait until the test job succeeds
quiz.explain: needs creates a dependency between jobs.

quiz.q: How should a deploy token be used in a workflow?
quiz.explain: Secrets are stored in GitHub and injected at run time, masked in logs.

Push it and open the **Actions** tab to watch it run. Then make it fail on purpose and see the red X on your commit.

modules.title: Production practice: safe releases and operations

lessons.title: Zero-downtime deploys
lessons.summary: Release new versions without users ever seeing an error page.

slides.title: The naive way
slides.text:
1. Stop old version
2. Start new version

Between 1 and 2 the site is **down**. With many deploys a day, that hurts.
slides.narration: The simplest way to deploy is to stop the old version and start the new one. But between those two moments, your site is down and users see errors. If you deploy many times a day, that adds up fast.

slides.title: Rolling update
slides.text:
Replace instances **one by one** behind a load balancer.

- Always some healthy instances serving
- Default in Kubernetes Deployments
- Old and new run side by side briefly
slides.narration: A rolling update replaces instances one at a time behind a load balancer. There are always healthy copies serving traffic. It is the default in Kubernetes. Note that for a short time the old and new versions run side by side.

slides.title: Blue-green
slides.text:
Two full environments:
- **Blue** = current live
- **Green** = new version, tested in place
- Switch the router: blue -> green in one step
- Rollback = switch back
slides.narration: Blue green deployment keeps two complete environments. Blue is live, and you deploy the new version to green and test it. Then you flip the router so all traffic goes to green at once. If something is wrong, you simply flip back.

slides.title: Canary releases
slides.text:
Send a **small slice** of traffic to the new version first:

1% -> 10% -> 50% -> 100%

Watch errors and latency at each step; stop if metrics get worse.
slides.narration: A canary release sends only a small slice of users to the new version, maybe one percent. You watch error rates and speed. If everything looks good, you increase to ten percent, then fifty, then everyone. If metrics get worse, you stop before most users are affected.

slides.title: Health checks and graceful shutdown
slides.text:
- **Readiness check**: only send traffic when the app is ready
- **Liveness check**: restart if stuck
- **Graceful shutdown**: on SIGTERM, stop accepting new requests, finish current ones, then exit
slides.narration: Zero downtime also needs health checks. A readiness check tells the load balancer when a new instance can take traffic. And when an old instance is stopped, it should shut down gracefully: stop taking new requests, finish the ones in progress, and only then exit.

slides.title: Database changes
slides.text:
**Expand and contract**:
1. Add new column (old code ignores it)
2. Deploy code that writes both
3. Backfill data
4. Deploy code that reads new
5. Remove old column later
slides.narration: The trickiest part is the database, because old and new code may run at the same time. The expand and contract pattern solves this. First add new structures without breaking old code, then move the code over in steps, and only remove the old column at the very end.

lessons.notes:
## Why it matters

Users expect services to be always available. If every deploy causes even 30 seconds of errors, teams deploy less often, and changes get bigger and riskier.

## Strategies

| Strategy | How | Pros | Cons |
|---|---|---|---|
| Rolling | replace instances gradually | simple, no extra capacity | two versions live at once |
| Blue-green | two environments, switch traffic | instant switch and rollback | double resources |
| Canary | small % of traffic first | limits blast radius | needs good metrics and routing |

**Feature flags** complement these: deploy code switched off, then turn features on for some users without redeploying (tools: LaunchDarkly, Unleash, Flagsmith, OpenFeature standard).

## Health checks

```js
app.get('/healthz', (req, res) => res.send('ok'));        // liveness
app.get('/readyz', async (req, res) => {                   // readiness
  const dbOk = await db.ping().catch(() => false);
  res.status(dbOk ? 200 : 503).send(dbOk ? 'ready' : 'not ready');
});
```

## Graceful shutdown

```js
process.on('SIGTERM', () => {
  server.close(() => process.exit(0)); // finish in-flight requests
});
```

## Database migrations

Old and new code overlap, so schema changes must be **backward compatible**. Use **expand and contract**:
1. Expand: add new column/table, nullable.
2. Deploy code that writes to both.
3. Backfill existing rows.
4. Deploy code that reads from the new place.
5. Contract: drop the old column in a later release.

Never rename or drop a column in the same deploy as the code that stops using it.

quiz.q: In a blue-green deploy, how do you roll back?
options: Switch traffic back to the old (blue) environment
quiz.explain: The old environment is still running, so you just switch back.

quiz.q: What is a canary release?
options: Sending a small share of traffic to the new version first
quiz.explain: Canaries expose a small group first to limit damage.

quiz.q: Why use expand-and-contract for database changes?
options: Old and new code may run at the same time, so the schema must work for both
quiz.explain: Backward-compatible steps avoid breaking the version still running.

lessons.task: Your app needs to rename the column `fullname` to `display_name`. Write the sequence of deploys (expand and contract) that does this with zero downtime. For each step say what the code and the database look like.

lessons.title: Rollbacks and recovering from bad deploys
lessons.summary: Plan how to undo a release fast when something goes wrong.

slides.title: Every deploy can fail
slides.text:
Even with tests, bugs reach production.

The question is not **if** but **how fast you recover**.

Mean time to restore (MTTR) is a key metric.
slides.narration: No matter how good your tests are, some bugs will reach production. Professionals accept this and focus on recovering quickly. The time it takes to restore service is one of the most important delivery metrics.

slides.title: Roll back vs roll forward
slides.text:
- **Roll back**: return to the previous known-good release
- **Roll forward**: ship a quick fix as a new release

Default: roll back first, investigate calmly after.
slides.narration: You have two choices. Rolling back means returning to the last version that worked. Rolling forward means shipping a quick fix. The safest default is to roll back first, so users are happy again, and then investigate without pressure.

slides.title: How to roll back
slides.text: Depends on your platform:
slides.narration: How you roll back depends on your tools. Hosting platforms usually have a button to promote an older deployment. Kubernetes has rollout undo. With Git you can revert the bad commit, and with containers you redeploy the previous image tag.
slides.code:
# Kubernetes
kubectl rollout undo deployment/web

# Git: create a commit that undoes another
git revert <bad-commit-sha>
git push

# Containers: redeploy previous tag
docker run ... myapp:1.4.1

slides.title: What makes rollback hard
slides.text:
- Database migrations that cannot be undone
- Data written in a new format
- Messages already sent (emails, payments)
- Mutable tags like `latest`
slides.narration: Some things make rollbacks hard. A migration that drops data cannot be undone. Data written in a new format may confuse the old code. Emails and payments cannot be unsent. And if you only use a tag like latest, you might not know which version was the previous one.

slides.title: Be ready before you need it
slides.text:
- Keep previous artifacts and immutable version tags
- Backward-compatible migrations
- Feature flags as a kill switch
- Practice the rollback
- Write a short **post-mortem** after incidents (blameless)
slides.narration: Prepare before trouble arrives. Keep older artifacts with exact version tags, write migrations that old code can live with, and use feature flags as a kill switch. Practice rolling back. After an incident, write a short blameless post mortem to learn from it.

lessons.notes:
## Recovery is a skill

The DORA research shows high-performing teams are not those that never fail, but those that **recover quickly**. A good rollback path turns a scary outage into a small blip.

## Roll back or roll forward?

- **Roll back** when the cause is unclear or the impact is large. It is usually the fastest way to restore service.
- **Roll forward** when the fix is tiny, well understood, and the pipeline is fast, or when rolling back is impossible (for example after an irreversible migration).

## Rollback methods

| Platform | Rollback |
|---|---|
| Vercel / Netlify / Render | "Promote" or "Rollback" to a previous deployment in the dashboard or CLI |
| Kubernetes | `kubectl rollout undo deployment/web` |
| Containers | redeploy the previous immutable tag, e.g. `myapp:1.4.1` |
| Git-based | `git revert <sha>` and let CI/CD deploy |
| Blue-green | switch traffic back |
| Feature flag | turn the flag off - no deploy needed |

## Make rollbacks safe

- **Immutable artifacts**: tag images with the version or commit SHA, never only `latest`.
- **Keep old releases** available for quick redeploys.
- **Backward-compatible migrations** (expand/contract), so old code still works with the new schema.
- **Automated rollback**: canary tools (Argo Rollouts, Flagger, cloud deploy services) can roll back automatically if error rates rise.

## After the incident

Write a **blameless post-mortem**: timeline, impact, root cause, what went well, and action items (for example "add a test", "add an alert"). Focus on improving systems, not blaming people.

quiz.q: What is usually the fastest way to restore service after a bad deploy?
options: Roll back to the last known-good release
quiz.explain: Rolling back restores a version that is known to work.

quiz.q: Why avoid deploying only with the `latest` tag?
options: It is mutable, so you cannot reliably redeploy the previous exact version
quiz.explain: Immutable version tags make rollbacks precise.

quiz.q: What does `git revert <sha>` do?
options: Creates a new commit that undoes the given commit
quiz.explain: revert adds an undo commit without rewriting history.

lessons.task: Write a one-page "rollback runbook" for an app you know: how to see which version is live, the exact command or button to roll back, how to verify it worked, and who to notify.

lessons.title: Monitoring, logs and alerts
lessons.summary: Know what your app is doing in production with logs, metrics, traces and alerts.

slides.title: You cannot fix what you cannot see
slides.text:
In production you have no debugger.

**Observability** = understanding the system from its outputs:
- **Logs** - what happened
- **Metrics** - how much / how fast
- **Traces** - where time went
slides.narration: In production you cannot attach a debugger and step through code. You need observability: the ability to understand your system from its outputs. The three pillars are logs, metrics and traces.

slides.title: Logs
slides.text: Write **structured** logs (JSON) to stdout:
slides.narration: Logs record events. Write them to standard output and let the platform collect them. Use structured JSON logs with fields like level, message and request ID, so you can search and filter them later. Never log passwords or personal data.

slides.title: Metrics: the golden signals
slides.text:
- **Latency** - how long requests take (p50, p95, p99)
- **Traffic** - requests per second
- **Errors** - percent of failed requests
- **Saturation** - CPU, memory, disk, queue length
slides.narration: Metrics are numbers over time. Google SRE suggests four golden signals: latency, traffic, errors and saturation. Watch high percentiles like p ninety nine for latency, because averages hide the slow requests that annoy users.

slides.title: Traces
slides.text:
A **trace** follows one request through many services:

`gateway 12ms -> auth 8ms -> orders 340ms -> db 310ms`

Standard: **OpenTelemetry**.
slides.narration: A trace follows a single request as it travels through many services, showing how long each step took. It quickly shows that, for example, a slow database query is the problem. OpenTelemetry is the open standard for collecting traces, metrics and logs.

slides.title: Alerts that matter
slides.text:
- Alert on **symptoms users feel** (error rate, latency), not every CPU spike
- Use **SLOs**: e.g. 99.9% of requests succeed over 30 days
- Every alert must be actionable
- Too many alerts = alert fatigue
slides.narration: Alerts wake people up, so make them count. Alert on symptoms that users feel, such as a high error rate. Define service level objectives, like ninety nine point nine percent of requests succeeding. Every alert should need a human action, or people learn to ignore them.

slides.title: Tools
slides.text:
- Metrics: **Prometheus** + **Grafana**
- Logs: Loki, Elasticsearch/OpenSearch, cloud logging
- All-in-one: Datadog, New Relic, Grafana Cloud, Honeycomb
- Errors: **Sentry**
- Uptime: external pings (UptimeRobot, Better Stack)
slides.narration: Popular tools include Prometheus and Grafana for metrics and dashboards, Loki or OpenSearch for logs, Sentry for application errors, and external uptime checkers that ping your site from around the world. Commercial platforms like Datadog combine everything.

lessons.notes:
## Observability

**Monitoring** tells you *that* something is wrong; **observability** helps you find out *why*. Three main signals:

1. **Logs** - timestamped records of events.
2. **Metrics** - numeric time series (requests/sec, error %, memory).
3. **Traces** - the path and timing of a single request across services.

**OpenTelemetry (OTel)** is the vendor-neutral standard for producing all three.

## Logging well

- Log to **stdout/stderr**; the platform ships logs to storage.
- Use **structured JSON** with consistent fields: `level`, `msg`, `time`, `requestId`, `userId` (if allowed).
- Use levels: `debug`, `info`, `warn`, `error`.
- Never log secrets, passwords, tokens or full card numbers; be careful with personal data (GDPR).

```js
console.log(JSON.stringify({ level: 'info', msg: 'order created', orderId, ms }));
```

## Metrics: golden signals

| Signal | Example |
|---|---|
| Latency | p95 response time 180 ms |
| Traffic | 1,200 requests/s |
| Errors | 0.3% HTTP 5xx |
| Saturation | 85% memory used |

## SLIs, SLOs and error budgets

- **SLI**: what you measure (share of successful requests).
- **SLO**: the target (99.9% over 30 days).
- **Error budget**: what is left (0.1% = about 43 minutes per month). If you burn it, slow down releases and fix reliability.

## Alerting

Page a human only for urgent, user-facing, actionable problems. Send everything else to a dashboard or ticket. Each alert should link to a **runbook** explaining what to do.

## Common stack

Prometheus + Grafana (metrics), Loki or OpenSearch (logs), Tempo or Jaeger (traces), Sentry (errors), plus an external uptime monitor. Managed options: Datadog, New Relic, Grafana Cloud, Honeycomb, and your cloud provider's built-in tools.

quiz.q: Which signal follows one request across several services?
quiz.explain: Traces show the path and timing of a single request.

quiz.q: Why prefer p99 latency over the average?
options: Averages hide the slow requests that users notice
quiz.explain: High percentiles reveal the slow tail of requests.

quiz.q: What makes a good alert?
options: Is about a user-facing symptom and needs a human action
quiz.explain: Good alerts are actionable and user-focused, avoiding alert fatigue.

lessons.task: For an app you know, define: two SLIs, one SLO with a number, three things you would log as structured JSON (with example fields), and one alert rule with the action a person should take when it fires.
